candidates.name: OpportunityInsights/EconomicTracker
candidates.what_it_holds: Official repo backing tracktherecovery.org. Committed CSVs (data/ folder) of Affinity-sourced credit/debit card consumer spending indices, indexed to a Jan 2020 base, split by spending category (Accommodation and Food Service, Arts/Entertainment/Recreation, General Merchandise, Grocery, Transportation, Retail excl. Auto/Gas, Health Care/Social Assistance, etc.), by income quartile (top/bottom), and by geography down to state, county and metro (CBSA) level; also employment (Paychex/Earnin/Womply), small-business revenue (Womply), and job postings (Burning Glass) series. Daily/weekly frequency, Jan 2020 to ~2022-2023 (tracker was discontinued but historical files remain committed); 341 stars, actively maintained fork activity as of Sep 2026 (updatedAt 2026-09-12). No explicit license field returned by API but repo states public/open data terms.
candidates.why_useful: Directly targets numbered gap #6 (public consumer-spend panels) and is exactly the named dataset (Affinity card spend). The 'Accommodation and Food Service' category series and county/metro-level granularity could proxy US regional travel/leisure consumer strength ahead of ABNB print dates, and the top/bottom income-quartile split speaks to who is still traveling. Caveat: series appears to stop around 2022-2023 based on tracker's known winddown, so it may not cover 2025-2026 guide-relevant quarters — needs verification of last data date before use.
candidates.size_hint: multiple CSVs, county/state-level panels, 341 GitHub stars
candidates.license: unspecified in API (check repo LICENSE file)

candidates.name: devashrlucas/OIET_Data_DB
candidates.what_it_holds: Third-party repackaging of the same Opportunity Insights Economic Tracker data 'as a database' (MIT licensed). Likely a SQL/SQLite ingestion of the same Affinity card-spend CSVs rather than new source data.
candidates.why_useful: Only useful as an alternative access format (queryable DB) if the primary OpportunityInsights/EconomicTracker repo's raw CSVs are hard to work with; adds no new data.
candidates.time_coverage: same as parent OI Tracker, unclear if kept current (last updated 2021)
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: duplicate of OpportunityInsights/EconomicTracker candidate above, and likely stale/outdated relative to it

candidates.name: itamarst/cambridge-dining
candidates.what_it_holds: Small analysis repo pulling OpenTable seated-diner year-over-year data for Cambridge, MA only.
candidates.why_useful: OpenTable seated-diners is explicitly named in gap #6 as a public consumer/leisure-spend indicator; this repo shows a working method to pull/parse it, even though scope (one city) is narrow.

candidates.name: imjakedaniels/restaurant_shutdown_toronto
candidates.what_it_holds: Year-over-year seated-customer counts from the OpenTable network for Toronto restaurants, limited to March 2020 (COVID shutdown period).
candidates.why_useful: Another OpenTable seated-diners method/dataset (gap #6), but the time window is a single month during COVID onset, so of limited use as a live consumer-strength proxy for 2026 forecasting.

candidates.name: itshyunseunglee/jeju-card-analysis
candidates.what_it_holds: Jeju Island (South Korea) regional card-spending dataset 2017-2018, used to analyze where/when a cafe would do well by area and time.
candidates.why_useful: A worked example of a national card-spend dataset by region/time outside the US/EU, structurally analogous to what a BBVA/CaixaBank/Norges Bank card panel would look like (regional card spend by merchant category); could serve as an APAC/Korea travel-adjacent consumer-spend proxy, though geography (Jeju, a tourist island) and vintage (2017-18) are dated and not KTO/travel-specific.

candidates.name: jimoholayinka01/Revolut-Spending
candidates.what_it_holds: End-to-end time series analysis/forecasting project on Revolut debit-card spending data in the UK, examining transaction trends by age demographic and seasonality. Not confirmed whether the underlying dataset is real Revolut transaction data, a public Revolut aggregate release, or a synthetic/Kaggle stand-in — needs a directory-listing check before relying on it.
candidates.why_useful: If the underlying data is genuine (even anonymized/aggregated) UK fintech card-spend data with seasonality, it is a private-sector analogue to ONS card spending (gap #6) for UK consumer strength, which reads on EMEA nights/ADR. Unverified provenance keeps this at medium-low until checked.

notes: Dead ends: gh search repos for 'SIBS card'/'Banco de Portugal', 'Norges Bank'/'Bank of England CHAPS', and 'track the recovery'/'affinity solutions spending' all returned irrelevant noise (generic payments SaaS, blockchain, budgeting apps) — no repos found for Portuguese SIBS card data, Norges Bank card statistics, Bank of England CHAPS, or BBVA/CaixaBank open research data via GitHub repo search; these central-bank/bank-research card panels do not appear to have GitHub mirrors, which is itself worth recording (a human should check if BBVA Research / CaixaBank Research publish CSVs on their own sites rather than GitHub, since none surfaced here). WebSearch was unavailable this session (session-wide 200/200 budget already exhausted before this scout ran) and WebFetch against github.com/search hit HTTP 429 rate limits (Retry-After 3600s), so site: search fallback could not be executed for ONS, Norges Bank, or BBVA/CaixaBank terms as instructed — a rerun of this theme with a fresh WebSearch budget or after the GitHub rate-limit window would likely surface more (e.g. any UK ONS 'Fable/faster indicators' GitHub Pages data pipeline, or academic replication repos citing SIBS/Banco de Portugal payment statistics). The one clear hit, OpportunityInsights/EconomicTracker, is a strong, well-known match for gap #6 but its data currently only confirmed back to the 2020-2022ish COVID tracker era — someone should verify in-repo whether the CSVs were kept updated into 2025-2026 (needed for point-in-time forecasting of the 5 Nov 2026 print) before treating it as usable, since our rule requires point-in-time/current data, not a frozen 2020-22 panel.
